papers.title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
papers.abstract: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.

papers.title: From Multi-site Kaplan-Meier Curves to Evidence Synthesis: An Empirical Evaluation of IPD Reconstruction and Reconstruction-Assisted Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Objective. To compare methods for reconstructing individual participant data (IPD) from Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves and evaluate their use when reported trial estimates are unavailable for meta-analysis. Materials and Methods. We compared iterative inverse-KM (iKM), IPDfromKM, KMtoIPD, and quadratic programming (QP) using their specified packages and auxiliary inputs. The single-trial benchmark evaluated curve agreement, event and risk-set accuracy, and treatment-effect accuracy across different survival settings. The meta-analysis benchmark compared omission of trials with unavailable estimates against four hybrid strategies that retained reported estimates and reconstructed missing estimates under missing-completely-at-random reporting. Results. Relative method performance varied by setting and accuracy measure. Accurate reproduction of curves or supplied risk tables did not consistently identify the smallest treatment-effect errors. In 30-trial meta-analyses with 80% of reported hazard ratios unavailable, hybrids retained 27.9-30.0 trials, compared with 6.0 for omission, and achieved pooled log-hazard-ratio root-mean-squared error of 0.0356-0.0371 versus 0.0852. Discussion. The comparisons reflect method-specific inputs, including accurately supplied auxiliary information, rather than algorithms receiving identical information. Controlled coordinate perturbation did not reproduce full image-digitization error. Conclusion. Reconstruction should be selected and evaluated for its intended analytical use. Under the tested conditions, hybrid strategies supported meta-analysis by supplementing unavailable compatible trial estimates.

papers.title: Score-aware nonparametric adaptation of prediction-powered inference
papers.abstract: Prediction-powered inference supplements labelled data with unlabelled data and external predictions to improve statistical efficiency. For inference on generalized linear model (GLM) coefficients, optimal use of these predictions generally requires estimating a conditional mean given the covariates and the external prediction, which can be challenging when the labelled data are limited or the covariates are multi-dimensional. We address this challenge through dimension reduction. We first fit an augmented generalized linear model combining the covariates and external prediction to obtain a scalar index, and then approximate the conditional mean by a univariate function of this index. Based on this construction, we develop a class of estimators for GLM coefficients and select the proposed estimator by minimizing the estimated asymptotic covariance trace. Under regularity conditions, the proposed estimator is asymptotically normal and has an asymptotic covariance trace no greater than that of the labelled-only estimator, even when the dimension reduction is insufficient. We also establish conditions under which the dimension reduction is sufficient. Simulations show that the proposed estimator is generally close to the best feasible estimator in root mean squared error, with confidence interval coverage close to the nominal level.

papers.title: CASPER: Discovering Spatially Resolved Causal Cell-Cell Communications
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics can reveal where ligands and receptors are expressed together. A harder question is whether exposure to a ligand changes pathway activity in nearby cells, since the same tissue environment can influence both ligand expression and pathway activity. We introduce CASPER, a Bayesian structural equation model that adjusts for receptor expression and represents the shared tissue environment with a Gaussian Markov random field. We show that the ligand-exposure effect is identifiable when the spatial covariance is known and distinguishable from independent noise, the coefficients are constant, and the structural errors are independent and homoskedastic. In simulations, CASPER reduced the bias seen in ordinary regression and in a regression that accounted for spatial dependence only in the outcome. We compared CASPER with CellPhoneDB in four public Xenium datasets. In ovarian cancer, CellPhoneDB found evidence of ligand--receptor expression enrichment for both IL6 and VEGFA. CASPER found greater support for a positive effect of fibroblast IL6 on the inflammatory-response score of ciliated epithelial cells than for an effect of fibroblast VEGFA on the angiogenesis score of endothelial cells. Code accompanies the Supplementary Materials and is available at https://github.com/nySTAT/casperCCC.

papers.title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.

papers.title: Revealing Geometry under Strong Noise: Spectral Embeddings and Clustering via Random Geometric Graphs
papers.abstract: Modern massive datasets often contain useful low-dimensional nonlinear structures that are hidden by noise. Spectral embedding algorithms rely on meaningful local relationships between observations, but noise accumulated across many coordinates can make the observed distances unreliable. This also complicates clustering when groups have curved or concentric shapes and cannot be distinguished by their centers. In this paper, we develop a new method that denoises pairwise distances before using them to construct spectral embeddings and identify communities. Our approach uses cross-fitted projections to estimate distances between the underlying signals, selects a neighborhood radius from the observed sample, and builds a random geometric graph whose spectral coordinates represent the latent geometric structure. By connecting nearby points, such a geometric graph can distinguish different groups even when their centers coincide. A novel recursive procedure is then proposed to extract clusters from the graph using its spectral embeddings when such clusters exist. On the theoretical side, under a manifold model, we provide guarantees for our spectral embedding algorithm, which can be understood through the eigendecomposition of an integral operator associated with the underlying geometry. We show that the algorithm is robust to noise when the total noise energy is comparable to the total signal energy or, under additional conditions, exceeds it. To our knowledge, this is among the first spectral embedding algorithms that can handle such strong noise in datasets with nonlinear structures. In addition, our proposed clustering algorithm can recover the underlying clusters even when their centers coincide. Numerical studies demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method in mitigating noise and revealing geometric structures for both spectral embedding and clustering.

papers.title: Triage Accuracy of Jev and Open-Weight System One Decision Models and Their Use for Early Emergency Recognition in Symptom-Assessment Applications
papers.abstract: Laypeople increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for triage advice, but LLMs answer in variable free text, which makes it hard to evaluate them for use in medical devices. Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synthetic cases correctly and agreed with an existing algorithm in 56.1% of real-world cases. They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. At a 5% error margin, it could decide for or against emergencies for about half of users. Decision models should therefore not replace triage engines but could shorten symptom assessments at setting-specific error margins.

papers.title: Spurious Information in Large Markets: Random Matrix Laws for Entropy, Mutual Information and the Value of Information
papers.abstract: Entropy, Kullback-Leibler divergence and mutual information have become standard currencies for measuring how much one set of financial variables reveals about another. In large cross-sections they are almost always computed from sample covariance matrices, and the noise in those matrices is the object of random matrix theory. This paper develops the random matrix theory of Gaussian information functionals and applies it to markets. I show that the plug-in mutual information between two blocks of p and r variables estimated from $n$ observations has an exact expected excess, the spurious information, that is a digamma telescope independent of the true dependence. Under independence its law is that of a product of Beta variables. In the proportional regime it grows linearly with an order-one variance. The same quantity is a linear spectral statistic of the Jacobi ensemble, which yields a closed form for the logarithmic moment of Wachter's law. Spurious information increases strictly whenever uninformative coordinates are added. In a CARA-Gaussian economy the certainty-equivalent value of a signal equals mutual information divided by risk aversion, so these results translate one for one into a spurious value of information. The canonical-correlation phase transition then defines a frontier of minimum detectable information. On daily returns of 49 US industry portfolios from 1990 to 2026, I document the market mode, the reliability of sector eigenvectors implied by the BBP transition, the out-of-sample cost of noise dressing, and an information linkage between carbon-intensive and financial industries that survives exact bias correction and conditioning on the market.

papers.title: $K$-Midranks: A robust clustering algorithm for heavy-tailed data with applications to spectroscopy and finance
papers.abstract: Clustering data with extreme observations and heavy tails can be challenging for methods that rely on distances between raw observations or specific distributional assumptions. We introduce $K$-midranks, a clustering method that replaces observations with coordinatewise ranks and partitions the transformed data using a procedure analogous to $K$-means. This transformation reduces the influence of extreme values while preserving the ordering of observations within each variable. We evaluate $K$-midranks against $K$-means, $K$-medoids, and mixture models based on Gaussian, Student's t, Cauchy, and generalized hyperbolic distributions through simulation studies, and provide some theoretical properties. $K$-midranks generally outperforms the competing methods on Cauchy-shifted data. In contrast, $K$-means and model-based methods perform better on Gaussian data and Student's t data with three degrees of freedom. We demonstrate the method's practical use in grouping samples based on Raman and LIBS spectra and clustering S\&P 500 stocks according to their returns. $K$-midranks achieves competitive performance with model-based methods in the spectroscopy applications and the best performance among the methods considered in the stock-return application. These findings suggest that $K$-midranks provides a useful alternative for clustering data with Cauchy-like heavy tails. An R package implementing the proposed method is available.

papers.title: Quantifying and calibrating precision gain from covariate adjustment in clinical trials with binary endpoints
papers.abstract: Covariate adjustment is widely used in randomized clinical trials to improve estimation and inference of treatment effects. For continuous endpoints, the reasoning is straightforward: prognostic baseline covariates explain outcome variability and thereby increase precision. For binary endpoints, however, the situation is more complex because conditional and marginal effects generally differ in nonlinear outcome models such as logistic regression. We develop a theoretical framework for quantifying the maximum attainable first-order precision gain from covariate adjustment when estimating marginal treatment effects for binary endpoints. We derive a closed-form identity showing that precision-gain potential is governed by an estimand- and allocation-specific combination of the treatment-specific risk functions. Building on this identity, we introduce marginal prognostic strength as a population-level measure of prognostic information and characterize when it determines precision-gain potential and when the two quantities decouple. Specifically, substantial prognostic information within both treatment arms need not translate into improved precision for the marginal treatment effect when covariates are predictive on the target effect scale. We further develop a calibration algorithm for methodological simulation studies that preserves prespecified conditional outcome structures and marginal risks while allowing data-generating mechanisms to be calibrated by marginal prognostic strength and evaluated in terms of estimand-specific precision-gain potential. Together, these results provide a theoretical and practical framework for understanding, quantifying, and calibrating potential precision gains from covariate adjustment for binary endpoints.

papers.title: Interpretable Discovery of Heterogeneous Causal Dose-Response Curves
papers.abstract: Discovering subgroups with heterogeneous treatment effects is a central task in causal inference. While methods for heterogeneous effect discovery have proliferated for discrete treatments, their counterparts for continuous treatments remain underdeveloped. In this paper, we introduce a novel, data-adaptive algorithm for discovering interpretable subgroups with heterogeneous causal dose-response curves. This algorithm combines doubly-robust dose-response curve estimation with recursive partitioning, using flexible objective functions to quantify heterogeneity across potential subgroups' dose-response curves. First, we show that the standard doubly-robust pseudo-outcome for continuous treatments cannot serve this purpose. We therefore construct the pseudo-outcome separately for each candidate subgroup, using subgroup-specific g-computation and a subgroup-specific stabilizing density. Finally, we characterize the differences between dose-response curves detected by each objective function. We establish uniform convergence of the splitting criteria and give conditions for recovery of the population greedy tree. We apply it to county-level data on fine particulate matter pollution (PM2.5) and mortality in the contiguous United States over the period 2000-2019. The discovered heterogeneous subgroups vary by education, income, and race. The proposed algorithm is implemented in the R package discoverHTE.

papers.title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
papers.abstract: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.

papers.title: Identification of Poisson processes through a one-dimensional projection
papers.abstract: We study the identification of stationary Poisson processes in Euclidean space through a single one-dimensional projection. Given a point process and a straight line, each point is retained independently with a probability given by a Gaussian function of its distance to the line; the retained points are projected onto the line. If the process is Poisson, the projection is again Poisson. What a single projection reveals depends on the sign of the second factorial cumulant, which is also the sign of the two-point correlations. Under a Palm domination condition, which holds for positively associated processes, the cumulant is nonnegative. Using a Chen-Stein argument we show that when the cumulant of the projection vanishes, the process is Poisson. Consequently, a single projection identifies non-Poissonianity. The same result holds under negative association. When the cumulant changes sign, a random projection detects a nonzero cumulant with probability one. We propose a test whose rejection region is computed by Monte Carlo. The test, together with a spacings-based variant for repulsive alternatives, rejects determinantal, shot-noise and other classical processes. When applied to lunar impact craters, the test rejects the Poisson hypothesis for craters with diameter below 30 km and does not reject it for craters above 45 km.

papers.title: Comparison of 3D-DXA Measurements with QCT Software Solutions for Proximal Femur Bone Density Assessment
papers.abstract: 3D-Shaper reconstructs proximal femur shape and density in 3D from a standard hip dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan. In men and women aged 35-91 years, we compared 3D-Shaper integral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), trabecular vBMD, and cortical surface BMD (sBMD) with quantitative computed tomography (QCT) processed with three methods: an in-house pipeline, Stradview and QCTPro CTXA, which were used to derive bone measurements equivalent to those of 3D-Shaper. Agreement, including among QCT methods, was assessed with linear regression and Bland-Altman analysis (bias and limits of agreement, LoA). 3D-Shaper agreed strongly with the in-house pipeline and Stradview for integral vBMD (R=0.95-0.96; bias 1.5 to 4.2 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$39.7 to 41.4 mg/cm$^3$), trabecular vBMD (R=0.92-0.94; bias -11.8 to -7.8 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$33.3 to 39.4 mg/cm$^3$) and cortical sBMD (R=0.94; bias 5.6 to 38.2 mg/cm$^2$; LoA $\pm$23.6 to 26.4 mg/cm$^2$). The in-house pipeline and Stradview agreed for integral vBMD (R=1.00; bias -2.7 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$3.7 mg/cm$^3$), trabecular vBMD (R=0.96-1.00; bias -0.2 to 3.9 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$6.9 to 27.5 mg/cm$^3$) and cortical sBMD (R=0.98; bias 32.7 mg/cm$^2$; LoA $\pm$14.6 mg/cm$^2$). Compared with 3D-Shaper, QCTPro CTXA integral vBMD was systematically lower (R=0.90; bias -28.4 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$61.5 mg/cm$^3$) and trabecular vBMD showed a proportional bias (R=0.89; bias -44.1 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$61.3 mg/cm$^3$). The same pattern was observed against the other QCT methods, for integral vBMD (R=0.93; bias -32.6 to -29.9 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$49.6 to 50.0 mg/cm$^3$) and trabecular vBMD (R=0.94-0.96; bias -36.3 to -32.5 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$51.2 to 54.9 mg/cm$^3$). These findings support the agreement of 3D-Shaper with independent QCT approaches and show that 3D-Shaper-QCT differences must be interpreted in light of the QCT method used.

papers.title: Transport-Safe Evaluation of LLM Agents: Trajectory-Dependent Judge Error and Anytime-Valid Auditing
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are often ranked by an LLM judge whose error rates are measured once and reused for every agent. The corrected success rates can then be biased when the judge's errors depend on the trajectory and agents differ in the trajectories they produce for successes or failures. We derive the exact asymptotic bias and give a chain of checks from identification to simultaneous ranks. On a four-agent semi-synthetic benchmark, a scalar correction with oracle calibration has maximum bias 0.245 and mean pointwise coverage 0.016, and never recovers the full ranking (0/250 replications). Augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with a uniform or a design-aware random audit keeps the maximum bias below 0.003, with mean pointwise coverage of 0.939 and 0.950. In a 48-cell stress test, effective target support rises only from 0.209 to 0.805 as calibration grows from 600 to 4,800 labels, while audited AIPW keeps a mean absolute error of 0.018-0.020. Without calibration support, or with judge dependence within an externally justified bound, we report valid bounds or sensitivity sets and carry them into rank sets. An e-process confidence sequence stays valid, for a stable target, under predictable adaptive auditing and arbitrary stopping.

papers.title: Bayesian sequential decision-making for adaptive early warning of bridge failure risk
papers.abstract: As a critical functionality of structural health monitoring (SHM) systems, early warning of increased bridge failure risk is essential for structural safety. However, traditional methods treat early warning merely as passive detection against a fixed safety limit and neglect evolving uncertainties and the economic consequences of decisions, leading to delayed alarms that increase the failure risk and hinder reliable and rational decision-making. This study formulates the early warning of increased structural failure risk as a sequential decision-making problem and develops a Bayesian framework for its solution. The presented framework unifies a probabilistic state transition model, an observation prediction model, cost models for early warning decisions, and a threshold-based decision strategy into a closed loop encompassing update, prediction, optimization, and decision execution. The structural state is updated iteratively via Bayes' theorem upon the arrival of new monitoring data, ensuring each decision is conditioned on the latest information. Through pre-posterior analysis over predicted future observations, the warning threshold is optimized by minimizing the expected total cost, which explicitly balances structural failure risks against warning response costs. In this way, the warning paradigm is shifted from passive detection to proactive decision-making, with the warning threshold adaptively updated as uncertainties and costs evolve. The framework was verified via two bridge case studies covering typical scenarios that lead to increased structural failure risk, including steel truss member fracture and stay cable rupture. Results demonstrate that warning decisions can be triggered in a timely and effective manner before severe consequences occur.

papers.title: Sequential Monitoring of Image Streams Using Energy Statistics
papers.abstract: Sequential monitoring of image data is a high-velocity, high-dimensional big data problem in statistics and machine learning, with wide applications in manufacturing industries, satellite imaging, medical diagnostics, and remote sensing. This is a challenging task because image intensity functions are often contaminated by noise and contain discontinuities and other complicated spatial structures. In the literature, a vast majority of image-monitoring methods rely on changes in image intensity values to detect out-of-control images. However, such approaches are often unreasonable in applications where insignificant changes in image contrast or background intensity should not indicate an out-of-control image as long as the boundaries of the image objects remain unchanged. In this article, we propose a nonparametric Phase II image-monitoring procedure based on energy distance that directly monitors changes in the distribution of image boundaries. The proposed method constructs a moving-window energy-distance-based control statistic by comparing the distribution of recently observed image boundaries with that of a fixed in-control reference sample. The central idea behind the proposed boundary-based approach is twofold: first, to reduce the dimensionality of high-resolution images by retaining relevant edge information, and second, to provide a robust monitoring procedure that is less sensitive to insignificant smooth changes in image intensity. The proposed construction offers a computationally efficient distributional approach to image monitoring without requiring a parametric model for out-of-control images. Theoretical justifications and superior performance in numerical comparisons ensure that the proposed control chart can be useful to many researchers and practitioners.

papers.title: Robust Mixture Regressions and EM Algorithms via the Log-Truncated Likelihood
papers.abstract: Finite mixture regression is sensitive to gross residual outliers when component errors are modeled by Gaussian likelihoods. We propose a log-truncated likelihood for mixture regression. The likelihood is obtained by integrating a logarithmically growing Catoni-type score and exponentiating the negative integrated score, producing a proper location-scale density with a reusable normalizing constant and EM-compatible responsibilities. Although the induced density itself is lighter than exponential and has all moments, its likelihood score grows only logarithmically; this distinction yields a smooth residual-robust estimator that can be stably fitted when the data are generated from Laplace, Pareto, or even infinite-variance heavy-tailed error mechanisms. We derive deterministic tail envelopes, the location-scale decomposition of the normalizing constant, a rejection sampler, a lower-bounded mixing-weight update, a unique componentwise scale update, and a constrained generalized EM algorithm. The theory gives monotonicity of the observed likelihood and a local population-to-sample perturbation guarantee under standard compactness, contraction, and numerical-accuracy conditions. Simulations and applications to insurance claim severity and crypto return innovations show that the method is a competitive smooth likelihood-based alternative to Gaussian and pseudo-robust EM procedures, especially in residual-outlier regimes, while also clarifying its limitations under high leverage and extremely adversarial contamination.

papers.title: What Environment Invariance Identifies: Minimal Invariant Sets in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
papers.abstract: Invariant causal prediction identifies the direct causes of a target $Y$ by searching for covariate sets whose conditional law of $Y$ is stable across environments. We state that criterion at the level of operators, calling a set $S$ invariant when the conditional mean embeddings of $Y$ given $X_S$ agree across environments, and characterise the resulting family exactly: under two conditions on the environments, which we state separately because they fail independently, the invariant sets are precisely those containing $PA(Y)$ and no descendant of $Y$. Two consequences follow. Invariance does not identify $PA(Y)$ uniquely, since every descendant-free superset is invariant as well; and $PA(Y)$ is the unique minimal invariant set. In finite samples, recovery requires the non-invariant sets to be separated from invariance by a margin, and the sample size splits into a screening term logarithmic in the ambient dimension and a term inherited from conditional mean embedding estimation, which is the binding one. The characterisation yields two selection rules with different failure modes, of which the conservative one controls false positives. Controlled experiments verify each population prediction directly, including the failure of uniqueness. They also show that invariance testing is a practical bottleneck: two natural designs are severely miscalibrated, while the selected test reduces but does not eliminate Type I error inflation.

papers.title: What Should an Experiment Measure? Combining a Short-Term Experiment with Confounded Observational Data to Identify Long-Term Treatment Effects
papers.abstract: Observational data often record long-term outcomes but do not identify long-term treatment effects when selection depends on unrecorded characteristics, while randomized experiments remove this selection but require years of follow-up. We ask what a short-term experiment should measure so that, combined with observational data, it identifies the average long-term treatment effect in the observational population. In our main setting, the observational data record a coarse post-treatment measurement of the unrecorded characteristics but not a detailed measurement that would remove confounding. In this setting, we derive three implications for what the experiment should measure. It should (1) collect the same coarse measurement, (2) measure the characteristics in enough detail that conditioning on this detailed measurement and recorded covariates removes confounding and leaves the coarse measurement uninformative about selection and the treatment-specific long-term outcome mean, and (3) distinguish no more levels of the characteristics than the coarse measurement can separate. We characterize the treatment effect through linear inverse problems based on exclusion restrictions and completeness, and thereby show that combining such an experiment with the observational data identifies the effect. We propose an estimator that is based on the efficient influence function and removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation errors. We give conditions under which this estimator is asymptotically normal and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Cross-fitting relaxes the conditions on nuisance estimation. In simulations and a Job Corps illustration, the proposed Tikhonov-penalized series estimator has smaller absolute bias and coverage closer to the nominal level than competing estimators.

papers.title: Adaptive experiments with observational data: Efficient experimental design and asymptotic time-uniform inference for long-term treatment effects
papers.abstract: Estimating long-term treatment effects in experiments requires waiting for outcomes to become observable, which can delay both the evaluation of an intervention and subsequent decisions. Recent econometric work has developed identification methods that combine experimental data with observational data containing long-term outcomes. This paper proposes using observational data available before the experiment begins not only for identification but also for designing adaptive experiments, in which experimental data are collected sequentially. To estimate the long-term average treatment effect as precisely as possible, we express its semiparametric efficiency bound as a function of the covariate sampling and treatment assignment rules and minimize the bound over these rules to characterize an optimal fixed experimental design. This experimental design depends on the treatment-specific conditional variances of the observational prediction of the long-term outcome, which can be learned only from experimental participants. We therefore construct a sequential procedure that learns the experimental design as experimental data accumulate and show that its estimator attains the same limiting variance as an oracle estimator implemented under the optimal fixed experimental design. We further construct an asymptotic confidence sequence whose coverage holds simultaneously over all rounds after a prespecified start, so that the experimenter can inspect the interval after each participant and stop once it excludes zero. Monte Carlo simulations show that the learned experimental design can improve precision and shorten the time to detection relative to baseline sampling and equal-probability assignment. An illustration using the Pakistan Graduation experiment shows how estimated conditional variance heterogeneity informs sampling and treatment assignment.

papers.title: Pesticide mixtures may compromise ecosystem services provided by an egg parasitoid of soybean pest stink bugs: a comprehensive ecotoxicological risk assessment
papers.abstract: Tank mixtures of crop protection products are widely used in agricultural systems, yet their integrated effects on biological control agents remain poorly understood. We evaluated the lethal, sublethal, and transgenerational effects of four synthetic insecticides, applied alone or in binary mixtures with three fungicides and two herbicides, on adults and pupae of Telenomus podisi (Hymenoptera: Scelionidae), an important egg parasitoid of pest stink bugs. In adult bioassays, LC50 values ranged from 28.26 mg a.i. L-1 for isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin to 265.88 mg a.i. L-1 for acephate. Overall, mixtures increased adverse effects relative to the individual products, reducing survival, parasitism, and longevity. The lowest parasitism rates occurred with isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin combined with chlorothalonil or glyphosate SL formulation. Transgenerational effects were also detected, including reduced F1 emergence and an increased proportion of males in some treatments. Following pupal exposure, several mixtures reduced F0 emergence, whereas ethiprole + fenpropimorph and acephate + bixafen + prothioconazole + trifloxystrobin also reduced parasitism and longevity of the emerged adults. Integration of lethal and sublethal responses using the reduction coefficient (Ex) revealed increased toxicity for several mixtures and shifts in IOBC risk classification; notably, all insecticide + glyphosate mixtures reached Ex = 100% after pupal exposure. These findings show that assessing pesticides individually may underestimate ecotoxicological risk to T. podisi and highlight the need to consider pesticide mixtures in integrated pest management programs.

papers.title: Spectral Regularization Beyond Ridge Regression
papers.abstract: We study Inclusive Ridge (IR), a two-parameter spectral regularization family that contains ridge regression as well as iterated Tikhonov regularization. We derive its exact finite-sample coefficient risk and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for increasing or decreasing the additional filter-shape parameter around the ridge baseline to locally lower risk. We show that oracle-tuned ridge is generically suboptimal within the IR family. Under joint divergence of the penalty and filter order, we show that a nondegenerate spectral limit exists precisely when their ratio converges to a positive finite constant, yielding a continuous exponential filter. Along the fixed effective-scale path, we also obtain an exact risk-difference comparison and explicit sufficient conditions under which both higher-order estimators and the exponential limiting filter strictly outperform oracle-tuned ridge. In this regime, IR becomes progressively less sensitive to perturbations in the absolute penalty parameter while retaining sensitivity to its effective spectral scale, and a plug-in coefficient-risk first-order condition coincides with a degrees-of-freedom-adjusted discrepancy equation. Numerical examples based on the Fredholm inverse problem, tomographic reconstruction, a regression design, and synthetic difference-in-differences donor-weight estimation illustrate both the potential gains and the limitations of feasible tuning, distinguishing oracle improvements from gains attainable with estimated tuning parameters.

papers.title: Tensor Recovery with Heterogeneous Mode Structures
papers.abstract: Tensor recovery methods often impose a common structural assumption across modes, even when different modes may exhibit distinct forms of regularity. We propose a unified convex framework that treats each mode according to its structure. Smoothly varying modes form an indexing domain and are handled by local kernel weighting, whereas retained modes may receive low-rank, group-sparse, graph-Laplacian, or autoregressive regularization in distinct and potentially overlapping combinations. The framework also covers ordinary tensor recovery without local smoothing. A consensus HM-ADMM algorithm separates the active penalties into tractable proximal and linear-system updates. For the population-quadratic estimator, we derive deterministic oracle inequalities and high-probability bounds under independent trace regression. The bounds disentangle stochastic error, rank and support complexity, smoothing bias, and quadratic mismatch. They also identify when quadratic penalties sharpen the Frobenius-error bound. For regular smooth domains, the theory characterizes the bias-variance trade-off and yields an optimal bandwidth order, with a specialization to uniform tensor completion. Simulations and two applications illustrate the gains from matching regularization to mode-specific structure, especially under severe undersampling.

papers.title: Assumptions, Modeling and Risks: Applying ICH M15 to Statistical Modeling
papers.abstract: In many instances in phase II and III clinical trials, critical assumptions underlying statistical analyses require discussion with regulators and other stakeholders. Such discussions benefit from a guiding process to promote consistency and clarity, but no widely and consistently applied framework currently exists. In January 2026, the International Council for Harmonisation released the ICH M15 Guideline on General Principles for Model-Informed Drug Development, which proposes a systematic framework for evaluating mechanistic models to support regulatory and development decisions. Although it focuses on mechanistic modeling, its structured assessment of model risks and benefits may be equally applicable to other approaches typically requiring a thorough appraisal of methodology and alignment among stakeholders, such as external data use and parametric longitudinal data analysis, and novel methodological approaches more generally. We illustrate and discuss how systematic risk-benefit evaluation of statistical models under the ICH M15 framework could work and propose its use to support acceptance of context-specific modeling strategies and to enhance decision-making transparency.

papers.title: How long must an honest confidence interval be after causal discovery? Benign and malignant weak edges
papers.abstract: After causal discovery, a confidence interval for a total effect valid uniformly over the model class must pay for structural uncertainty. We measure this price by the worst-case ratio of expected length to that of the efficient interval knowing the graph, for linear Gaussian models with a known superset of the adjacencies and k-triangle faithfulness. The global price is of order sqrt(n) once one edge can be malignant, so we study it locally, near a generic distribution with one edge absent. Our main result classifies this weak edge by Meek closures. It is benign if deleting it leaves the effect identifiable in the resulting MPDAG and Markov equivalent explanations agree; the local price is then bounded, and otherwise, for small k, of order sqrt(n). At benign edges the price is of order R+K, with R a ratio of efficient lengths and K a cross-model constant. It equals one, so that honesty is free, exactly when K = 0, generically decided by a d-separation. For two Markov classes it is determined within a factor 3.40, and its upper bound is approached without knowing the base point or the weak edge. A further graphical condition gives the rate uniformly in a second edge's margin.

papers.title: Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.

papers.title: Empirical Null Estimation via Adaptive Shifting and Tail Reconstruction for Large-Scale Multiple Testing
papers.abstract: Dependence among test statistics can produce complex empirical null shapes that are poorly captured by conventional parametric models. We propose TRAIL (Tail Reconstruction via Adaptive Iterative Learning), a method that estimates the pooled conditional null under a Gaussian factor model using a Gaussian-Hermite expansion without requiring the null correlation matrix as input. The procedure progressively reconstructs the potentially contaminated tail by generating pseudo-observations and retaining them in successive blocks from the initial cutoff outward. Its implementation, TRAIL_BIC, jointly selects the Gaussian reference location and Hermite truncation order using a BIC-type criterion. We characterize its limiting behavior and establish pooled-null consistency, together with asymptotic false discovery rate control and recovery of pooled oracle power under suitable conditions. Simulations across diverse dependence structures and null shapes show generally more stable false discovery behavior than competing empirical null methods with competitive power. An application to 48 coronary artery disease studies illustrates the method's flexibility in capturing complicated empirical shapes and its ability to identify more discoveries on average than the competing empirical null procedures.

papers.title: The Entangled Veil: Why Redistribution Requires a New Language
papers.abstract: The Rawlsian veil of ignorance requires choosing principles of justice without knowing which position-temporal, spatial, social, or personal one will occupy. We argue that this object cannot be represented faithfully within standard economic models. A faithful representation must satisfy three requirements: it must treat all generations symmetrically, capture non-separable correlations among positions, and allow mobility costs to vary across locations and occupations. We show that standard optimal-tax models violate at least one requirement, and that the minimal framework satisfying all three is a geometric framework adapted from string theory, in which the veil is an entangled state over a space of possible life situations. We derive full equalization as a first-best benchmark, the emergence of separated clusters when correlations reward distinction, a symmetry between intraand inter-generational equity, and a tunneling mechanism by which correlations reduce institutional barriers. The model generates four inequality profiles and four inequality types. The estimates are quantitatively important: the framework changes the ranking of redistributive policies, and ignoring the margins it identifies leads to systematically biased policy evaluation.

papers.title: Model-Assisted Probability of Detection Studies for Image-Based Human Inspection
papers.abstract: Establishing a probability of detection (POD) curve is important for assessing the reliability of components in aging systems. Traditional POD studies rely on physical specimens containing representative flaws and human inspectors who record detection results, making such studies costly. This paper demonstrates how appropriately validated physics-based simulation can substantially reduce, and in suitable applications potentially replace, physical POD experiments. We use XRSIM, an X-ray radiographic simulator, to generate weld images containing cracks of varying size, morphology, and location. Flaw characteristics, locations, and the number of flaws per image were randomized, with images containing zero to three flaws. Each simulated flaw is treated as an observational unit contributing flaw-level hit-miss responses. To capture human inspection variability, the images were presented in random order to five inspectors, each of whom inspected the images twice. The resulting data were analyzed using a repeated-measures binary-regression model accounting for flaw-to-flaw, inspector-to-inspector, flaw/inspector-combination, and inspection-to-inspection variability. Bayesian inference was used to estimate the population-mean POD curve, inspector-specific POD curves, and associated statistical uncertainty. Results show that flaw-to-flaw variability dominates, with appreciable differences among inspectors. The study provides a framework for combining physics-based image simulation with controlled human inspection to estimate POD while reducing the experimental burden of physical specimen fabrication.

papers.title: Discovery-Targeted False Discovery Rate Control
papers.abstract: In exploratory multiple testing, the false discovery rate (FDR) is a commonly used error criterion, and existing methods typically take an FDR level and return a set of discoveries. However, scientists often begin with a target number of discoveries, and accept any FDR level below a reasonable upper limit. Motivated by this practical need, we develop an FDR control approach with a data-driven, discovery-targeted level, which uses synthetic null p-values to split the p-value information between level selection and multiple testing. For independent p-values, the proposal controls finite-sample FDR given the reported level, which can therefore be interpreted in the standard way of a prespecified level. Asymptotically, the number of discoveries and the reported FDR level converge to the target and the optimal value. We also extend the approach to conformal p-values and to include a null proportion estimate. In simulations and real-data examples, the procedure yields a number of discoveries close to the target and smaller FDR levels compared with methods based on e-values or simultaneous false discovery proportion bounds.

papers.title: Sequential Selection against an Adaptive Opponent
papers.abstract: Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent adapts to what it observes, so a strategy that keeps winning in practice may already have stopped working by the time it is used. Motivated by these settings, we study a player who tries strategies in practice games against an adaptive opponent, decides when to stop, and then either selects one strategy for the next game or abstains. The goal is to select a strategy that meets a target win probability while rarely selecting one that has already fallen below it. For a single strategy, we propose the Sequential Private Accumulated-excess Rule (SPAR), which accumulates evidence through a capped likelihood ratio and selects the strategy once this evidence reaches a privately drawn uniform threshold. We show that the stopping time must involve such private randomness. The number of games SPAR needs is inversely proportional to the error tolerance, and this rate is optimal even when the opponent happens not to adapt. To select among multiple strategies, we introduce Screen-then-SPAR, which screens candidates in stages before applying SPAR. The procedure adapts to the best strategy's unknown initial margin above the target and achieves the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. The performance of Screen-then-SPAR is demonstrated through simulations and two real-data studies, one using recorded coding-agent attacks from MonitoringBench and the other using rock-paper-scissors matches between human players and an adaptive bot.

papers.title: Space-Time Covariance with Screening Effects, Markov Property, and Long-Range Dependence
papers.abstract: Constructing space-time covariance models is an essential task to account for spatio-temporal dependence. However, there is a lack of practical guidance for constructing new covariance constructions. This paper focuses on studying the interplay among three statistical properties: screening effect, Markov property, and long-range dependence for constructing desirable parsimonious space-time covariance functions. While these properties imply seemingly conflicting statistical practice, it is shown in this paper that closed-form parsimonious covariance functions that simultaneously possess all these properties could be constructed and may be desirable for understanding space-time dependence. To examine these properties, this paper first shows that the confluent hypergeometric (CH) covariance function has asymptotic screening effect even in long-range dependent regime. Then this paper provides theoretical characterizations on Markov property for the hierarchical mixture construction including a necessary and sufficient condition. To account for more practical structures, this paper constructs a flexible Lagrangian CH model with the time-lag varying smoothness and tail decay parameters via a hierarchical mixture approach. These properties are illustrated via simulation studies. The practical performance under these models is evaluated for the Irish wind data and the sea surface temperature data.

papers.title: GABIF: An Adaptive Guided Graph Denoising Framework for Antibody Conditional Inverse Folding
papers.abstract: Antibodies play a central role in the human immune system, and their design is critical for vaccine development, therapeutic intervention, and improving human longevity. However, the vast combinatorial search space of antibodies poses a fundamental challenge for de novo discovery. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly denoising diffusion models, have demonstrated strong potential in protein inverse folding. Nevertheless, existing approaches are largely constrained to learning from natural antibody repertoires, thereby generating sequences that closely resemble natural antibodies. Such similarity, however, does not necessarily translate into improved functional performance in downstream applications. In this work, we develop a novel generative protein design model that enables the generation and optimization of antibody sequences tailored to specific downstream tasks and target metrics. Besides training on given an antibody dataset, we guide the generative model by an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor for conditional discrete diffusion. The model is pre-trained on a given antibody dataset. Meanwhile, an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor is incorporated as a conditional signal in a discrete diffusion framework, where a regressor serves as the conditional probability to guide the learning of the amino acid probability distribution of sequences under the objective of affinity optimization. In silico experiments demonstrate that our antibody design model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, while the proposed regressor effectively improves binding affinity, as validated by an independent external predictor. Furthermore, our results highlight that the combination of finetuning and supervised guidance provides a powerful paradigm for adapting pretrained models to downstream tasks.

papers.title: A Tensor Neural Network for Interpretable and Predictive Representations
papers.abstract: Tensor regression is challenged by the exponential dimensionality of tensor-valued covariates and their complex multi-mode dependence. Existing methods therefore often rely on simple models, such as linear tensor regression and tensor additive models, which are computationally tractable but impose restrictive structural assumptions and may limit predictive accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose a tensor neural network that learns low-dimensional, interpretable, and prediction-sufficient representations while preserving the multi-mode structure of tensor data. The model captures nonlinear effects for accurate response prediction while retaining the interpretability of classical linear tensor regression. Theoretically, we establish selection consistency for the minimal representation dimension $K^*$ necessary for prediction and show that the estimator attains a representation-adaptive non-asymptotic error rate. Specifically, the rate improves from the ambient-dimensional order $n^{-\fracβ{\mathcal{D}+2β}}$ to $n^{-\fracβ{K^*+2β}}$, where $\mathcal{D}=\prod_{j=1}^M P_j$ is the ambient dimension. This demonstrates that recovering the low-dimensional representation is crucial for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in tensor regression. Moreover, minimizing the derived generalization error bound yields explicit tuning-parameter choices for computationally lightweight tuning. Extensive simulations and real-data analyses show consistent performance across settings of varying complexity. Unlike black-box deep learning models, the framework supports direct visualization and interpretation of learned tensor representations without external post hoc tools.

papers.title: Identification multiplicity across study designs
papers.abstract: The answer to a causal question often admits several translations in terms of observed data. These may differ in adjustment sets, comparison groups, instruments, mediators, cutoffs, eligibility occasions, or data sources. We describe the resulting collection of analyses by three structures: the causal target that each analysis identifies under its assumptions, the assumptions that the analyses share, and the sampling dependence among their estimates. A single decomposition separates identification discrepancies from differences in causal targets, and we make both terms explicit in fourteen examples spanning adjustment, comparative panels, proxies, mediators, instruments, discontinuities, staggered adoption, sequential trials, and source combination. Comparisons within a collection can reveal differential violations of assumptions but not a bias common to all analyses; agreement is therefore evidence about the assumptions that differ, not about those that are shared. Averaging retains a causal interpretation in three ways: efficient combination of analyses that identify one target, a projection of a causal curve with a declared approximating family and weighting measure, and inference under weaker premises such as validity of at least one analysis or a known sign of its bias. Precision weights, regression-implied weights, and hierarchical models do not supply these interpretations by themselves. We relate this account to triangulation, overidentification, marginal treatment effects, transportability, and recent methods for inference under model uncertainty, and distinguish identification multiplicity from multiple testing.

papers.title: Topological Pharmacokinetics: A Model-Free Framework for Quantifying the Shape of Concentration-Time Curves
papers.abstract: Pharmacokinetic analysis compresses concentration-time curves into scalar summaries (non-compartmental analysis, NCA) or pre-specified compartmental models, approaches that are either model-free but shape-blind or shape-sensitive but structure-dependent. We introduce Topological Pharmacokinetics (TPK), a framework that reads curve shape directly from data without committing to any model. TPK delay-embeds each curve into a state-space trajectory and applies persistent homology to extract a nine-component topological invariant: multi-scale shape descriptors (peak hierarchy, secondary-peak isolation, loop structure) with established perturbation-stability properties. We evaluate the framework on four layers of increasing realism. Monophasic linear systems generate no spurious cyclic signals, whereas double-site absorption and enterohepatic recirculation produce distinct loop signatures; 12 nonlinear scenarios resolve as curvature-without-cycles; a weak endogenous rhythm survives superposition with a large exogenous drug signal (inter-peak interval recovered at exactly 24 h); and loop detection stays stable to 10 percent of Cmax additive noise and to sampling thinned to 7 points. As clinical proof of concept, we apply the same pipeline to 15 mycophenolic acid profiles digitized from a published kidney-transplant study. The secondary-persistence ratio associates with ex vivo gut-microbiome reactivation at Spearman rho = 0.815 (p = 0.0002, q = 0.002), whereas the tested exposure metrics show weak, nonsignificant associations (rho <= 0.38). Analyses are fully automated and reproducible; code and data are public. TPK is proposed as a complementary, model-free, shape-sensitive layer alongside NCA and model-based methods.

papers.title: The Coupled Scaled Dirichlet Distribution
papers.abstract: We introduce a coupled scaled Dirichlet distribution for paired compositions that may have different dimensions. Building on the matched Gamma-sharing construction of Trick, Rothkopf, and Jäkel (2023) for ordinary Dirichlet vectors, we allow scaled Dirichlet margins and extend the construction to include crossed sharing between non-corresponding latent components. We propose a signed coupling parameter whose sign selects matched or crossed sharing and whose magnitude controls the strength of sharing. We then develop a time-varying extension in which observed covariates determine this parameter. The model can therefore switch between matched and crossed sharing over time while preserving both scaled Dirichlet margins. We derive the joint mixed moments and use them to estimate dependence after fitting the margins separately. The moments can be evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation or by two-dimensional numerical quadrature, regardless of the dimensions of the compositions. Simulations show that the estimator generally recovers the sharing pattern, although weak crossed sharing is harder to detect. In an application to four U.S. equity-index futures, the time-varying model modestly improved the held-out energy and variogram scores for the trading-volume and intraday price-range compositions relative to the static-dependence model.

papers.title: Computational Strategies for Mixed Logit Estimation Automatic Differentiation, GPU Computing, and Floating-Point Precision
authors: Hengzhe Zhao Jinhui Zhang Yuanyuan Gu
papers.abstract: Mixed logit estimation can become computationally demanding as sample size and the dimension of preference heterogeneity increase. This study examines how derivative computation, processor choice and floating-point precision affect estimation time and parameter recovery across problem sizes. This paper provides a controlled benchmark, comparing finite differences (FD) with automatic differentiation (AD), central processing unit (CPU) execution with graphics processing unit (GPU) execution, and double-precision (FP64) with single-precision (FP32) arithmetic using Monte Carlo experiments that hold the data-generating process, simulation draws, optimiser, starting values, and objective function fixed across strategies. The results show that AD is the dominant source of acceleration. Combining AD with FP32 arithmetic provides further gains, while combining AD, GPU execution, and FP32 arithmetic delivers the largest speed improvements, particularly as sample size and model complexity increase. Our findings indicate substantial computational gains with broadly comparable parameter-recovery performance in the simulated settings considered.An empirical application in health preferences illustrates what extra empirical evidence and statistical benefit on model fit could be achieved, when researchers are made possible to estimate a richer, correlated preference specification. We provide an open sourced prototype to for model estimation with AD-FP32 strategy workflow that automatically detect hardware and provide the fastest estimation. Faster estimation can make richer random-coefficient specifications, larger simulation draw counts, bootstrap inference, multi-start optimisation, and robustness checks more feasible in applied choice modelling research.

papers.title: Shadow economy as a null set. Measure-theoretic approach to shadow economy
papers.abstract: In this paper we asked if the shadow economy can be defined as a system of null sets for institutional measures or sensors that measure economic transactions. As an answer a measure-theoretic testable framework to redefine and quantify the shadow economy was designed. Traditional economic definitions frequently conflate the actual shadow economy with the observational limitations of state institutions. To resolve this, we model the shadow economy as a null set relative to institutional measures and analyze three complementary economic regimes. We explore in this context how standard mathematical tools can be given economic meaning. First, in the low-resolution regime, we apply Banach Lattices and Lebesgue decomposition of a measure to address transaction underreporting by aggregating incomplete institutional registries using a supremum fusion operator. Second, for hidden economic dimensions, we utilize Copula theory and Kullback-Leibler divergence optimization to reconstruct unobserved financial flows from technological and physical indicators. Third, we address audit scalability by modeling the shadow economy as a sparse vector, applying Compressed Sensing to detect high-volume sparse evasion networks through random, incoherent, and privacy-preserving sampling.

papers.title: Model-Averaged Shrinkage Estimation of the Spectral Density Using Welch's Method
papers.abstract: We propose a shrinkage estimator of the spectral density based on a three-level hierarchical model. At the first level, we smooth Welch's spectral density estimator and model it as arriving from a Gaussian distribution centered at the true spectral density. In the second level, we place a normal prior on the true spectral density. We center this prior at a spectral density estimated assuming the data from an ARMA($p$,$q$) process. From these two levels, we create a conditionally specified shrinkage estimator. The conditional specification, of course, is the order of the ARMA process, i.e., the values of $p$ and $q$. We avoid selecting a particular order by creating a third level in which priors are placed on $p$ and $q$. Our final estimator is then a weighted average of shrinkage estimators. The average is taken over a set of ARMA($p$, $q$) models, and the weights are governed by the posteriors of $p$ and $q$. The methods introduced in this paper are similar to those presented in Botts and Daniels, but distinct from them in one critical way: the first level of the hierarchy. In the first level of our model, we borrow from recently developed theoretical results of Welch's spectral density estimator. Our estimator is consistent, computationally simple, and has performance comparable (and often superior) to other estimators.

papers.title: Sharpe Ratio Inference after Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The economic value of return signals is often assessed using the Sharpe ratios of portfolios based on those signals. In modern asset pricing, return signals often depend on many features, including state variables and firm-specific characteristics, and machine-learning methods are increasingly used to estimate them. But how much confidence can we place in the estimated Sharpe ratios? We find that signal-estimation error can remain consequential for inference even in large asset panels. Moreover, pooling observations across assets does not necessarily make this uncertainty negligible when predictors contain common features or exhibit substantial cross-sectional dependence. As a remedy, we develop a debiased Sharpe-ratio estimator that accounts for signal-estimation error and provides valid confidence intervals and tests against benchmarks. Our target is the population Sharpe ratio of a specified portfolio rule evaluated at the true conditional expected returns given the features. The framework covers market-timing, long-short, and other signal-based portfolios, allowing the number of assets to grow with and greatly exceed the time-series sample size. The method combines orthogonal portfolio moments with time-series cross-fitting and remains valid under suitable estimation-error bounds for machine-learning forecasts. Empirically, we revisit the setting of Gu et al. (2020) using machine-learning estimators of the return signals. The strongest long-short Sharpe-ratio gains relative to market benchmarks remain significant after debiasing, providing statistical evidence of the economic value of their feature set. Conventional and debiased Sharpe-ratio estimates are generally similar, while the associated confidence intervals and tests can differ substantially. These differences vary across signal estimators and portfolio rules and do not uniformly weaken the evidence of portfolio performance.

papers.title: Directed Hypergraphs: Tensor Representation, Embedding Modeling, and Community Detection
papers.abstract: Directed hypergraphs, in which each hyperedge connects a set of tail nodes to a set of head nodes, are the natural representation for many-to-many interactions in citation networks, metabolic pathways, and group communications. Despite their broad applicability, community detection for directed hypergraphs remains statistically underdeveloped: most existing methods either collapse hyperedges into pairwise edges, treat the two sides as interchangeable, or require the number of communities to be known. We propose a statistical framework for simultaneous embedding and community detection in nonuniform directed hypergraphs. The method allows each node to have distinct roles as a source and as a target, accommodates varying hyperedge sizes, and automatically determines the unknown numbers of communities on both sides, which need not be equal, through a fusion-penalized likelihood. We establish consistency of the estimated numbers of communities, exact recovery of both membership structures, and consistent probability tensor estimation. We further show that exact recovery is attainable without knowing the numbers of communities by a procedure that does not rely on any particular local solution, and we complement the upper bounds with a minimax lower bound for probability tensor estimation and a necessary condition for exact recovery. To ground the methodology, we construct the Cross-Statistics Citation Network, a new large-scale corpus linking Statistics with Biology, Computer Science, and Economics. Applying our method to this corpus reveals source and target roles of author communities in cross-field knowledge flow, and a pairwise representation of the same citations partly merges these roles.

papers.title: Probability-Feasible Historical Transport: Sharp Bounds and Falsification Tests for Distributional Pre-Trend Designs
papers.abstract: Distributional difference-in-differences studies often assume that the post-policy gap between treated and comparison groups is a mixture of pre-policy gaps. This historical-transport assumption can fail in ways that one-statistic checks miss. When policy events are pooled, the average counterfactual can be a valid distribution although no event's counterfactual is, and pooled bounds can exclude the true average effect. Mixtures of past gaps can assign negative probability to outcomes, and cutoff-by-cutoff bounds can be incompatible. We characterize sharp bounds and give breakdown radii, a grid-free confidence region, and tests with and without an experiment. The tests reject transport in the National Supported Work data and expose impossible state counterfactuals behind a pooled minimum-wage bound. For the 1993 Earned Income Tax Credit expansion they pass through 1995, when bounds put single mothers' employment gain relative to childless women at 5 to 7 points; the gain stays positive after dropping early welfare-waiver states.

papers.title: Bayesian Calibration of Computer Experiments and Extrapolation
papers.abstract: Calibration, a fundamental inverse problem in uncertainty quantification, suffers from model identifiability issues. While the discrepancy decomposition model partially addresses this via a first-order Taylor expansion, it struggles when the approximation is biased. We propose a Bayesian modified discrepancy decomposition model that incorporates a residual process to capture higher-order discrepancy structures. By jointly inferring calibration parameters and model discrepancies within a Bayesian framework, our model recovers more physically meaningful parameters and provides reliable uncertainty quantification. Crucially, this accurate parameter recovery enables reliable extrapolative prediction, a challenge current methods largely fail to address. We validate the approach through numerical studies and a real-world industrial application: predicting the thermal stability of multilayer mirrors in extreme ultraviolet lithography. In this application, our method accurately predicts high-temperature responses far beyond the training domain, significantly outperforming existing calibration methods.

papers.title: Exact, narrow and fast: Use the Gaffke confidence interval for the mean of a discrete bounded variable
papers.abstract: Survey ratings, test scores and many other data take a few known values, and we often want a confidence interval for their mean. For small samples, or for means close to the smallest or largest value, the usual intervals cover the true mean much less often than they claim. The interval of Gaffke generalizes the Clopper-Pearson interval to any finite set of values, and a recent proof of Gaffke's conjecture shows that its coverage is at least the nominal level for every sample size and every distribution. Its endpoints, however, are quantiles of a weighted sum of Dirichlet variables, with no closed form. This note makes three contributions. First, a fast and accurate algorithm for the endpoints: a Fourier inversion integral on a line through the saddle point gives tail probabilities with a small relative error, a Gauss-Legendre rule on geometric panels converges at the same rate wherever the singularities are, and a Newton iteration needs 2.6 evaluations per endpoint on average. The cost is $O(kN)$ operations for $k$ values and $N$ quadrature nodes, and $N$ does not grow with the sample size, so an interval takes less than a millisecond for any $n$. Second, an experimental comparison with the published intervals: for $n \le 30$, the Gaffke interval is the shortest of the intervals that keep the level, 17 to 20% shorter than the betting interval of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas and 19 to 37% shorter than Anderson's, while the shorter intervals (Wald, Student, profile likelihood, Bayesian) cover the mean less than 50% of the time for some distributions. Third, tested Python and R packages and a web page, with endpoints accurate to $10^{-12}$ of the range of the values. So the interval is exact, narrow and fast, and we recommend it.

papers.title: Pharmacy stock and post-earthquake access to medicines in Tokyo: modeling choices that change recovery judgments
papers.abstract: Community pharmacies sustain access to medicines after an earthquake only while open, staffed and stocked. Accessibility models rarely represent stock depletion, and the assumptions this requires may change conclusions about recovery. We examine these assumptions for over-the-counter (OTC) medicines supplied by 4,748 registered pharmacies in Tokyo's 23 wards during the first week after a magnitude-7.3 scenario earthquake. A two-step floating catchment area model computes walking accessibility for 2,651 grid cells (500 m) under 10,000 sampled combinations of stock duration, staffing, operation and demand. Results are expressed as Retention: post-disaster accessibility divided by the same cell's pre-disaster accessibility. First, the assumed link between stock and service, the supply a pharmacy can still provide, determines the recovery verdict. If service falls in proportion to remaining stock, mean Retention declines from 0.479 (days 2-3) to 0.273 (days 4-7). If service is maintained until stock falls below one quarter, the mean rises instead, although low-end (10th-percentile) outcomes still decline. Measuring at the start of each period rather than averaging over it also reverses the trend. Second, a simple model that rescales a fixed map by citywide supply and demand reproduces citywide patterns but cannot evaluate where pharmacies close or where capacity is added; a spatial model run once on average inputs can. Third, four floating catchment methods agree on overall rankings (rank correlation 0.81), but their lowest-ranked 10% of cells overlap only partially (Jaccard index 0.56). Disaster assessments should report stock assumptions and low-end outcomes, and treat local priority areas as method-dependent.

papers.title: Motivo: A Motif-Based Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Fast and Energy-Efficient Graph-Based Genome Analysis
papers.abstract: Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Motivo-ASIC provides 7.4-11.7x (138-274x) speedups over state-of-the-art CPU-based tools for short (long) reads. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

papers.title: Checking the Cumulative Exposure Model: Cumulative Chi-Squared Goodness-of-Fit Tests for Interval-Monitored Step-Stress Life Tests
papers.abstract: In an interval-monitored step-stress life test the data are the numbers of devices that fail between consecutive inspections. These cells are ordered in time, but the usual goodness-of-fit check, Pearson's statistic, ignores the order. We propose goodness-of-fit tests based on the cumulative residuals, the differences between the empirical and the fitted distribution functions at the inspection times, with the parameters estimated by the minimum density power divergence estimator. The two statistics are Taguchi's cumulative chi-squared statistic and its version with constant weights, the classical members of a family of cumulative divergences for ordered categories, with the null probabilities replaced by those of the fitted model. For the exponential cumulative exposure model with a log-linear link we prove the existence, uniqueness and consistency of the estimator under explicit conditions, and we derive the limit distribution of the statistics under the null hypothesis and under contiguous alternatives: a weighted chi-square distribution with $L-s$ terms, where $L$ is the number of inspection times and $s$ the number of parameters. The critical values are obtained by plugging the estimated weights into Imhof's formula, and the procedure has asymptotic size $α$. A local-power analysis and a simulation study show that the cumulative statistics are more powerful than Pearson's statistic against a wrong lifetime distribution, and that the limit distribution is accurate already with $50$ devices. An application to light bulbs tested under step voltage illustrates the method.

papers.title: Community Detection in Fuzzy Social Networks through Fuzzy Co-Membership Relations over Alpha-Cut Realizations
papers.abstract: In fuzzy social networks the ties between actors are triangular fuzzy numbers, and community detection applied to their cores ignores how the partition depends on their vagueness. We propose a fuzzy co-membership relation obtained by running the Louvain algorithm on crisp networks compatible with the alpha-cuts of the ties and integrating the proportions of co-assignment over alpha. The relation is positive semidefinite; from it we derive a consensus partition, the number of groups, membership degrees and an assignment ambiguity index. In simulations from stochastic block models the relation does not yield better partitions than symmetric perturbations of the cores of the same size. Its ambiguity index is more closely associated with the structural position of the actors and identifies actors split between two groups when the vagueness is concentrated on them; when the asymmetry of the fuzzy ties points towards the latent tie strength, its co-membership degrees have a lower Brier score. The interval-weighted Louvain algorithm estimates the number of communities more accurately. In two departmental collaboration networks the observed ambiguity is lower than under permuted ratings, while the partitions depend on the symmetrization of directed ratings and on the coding of non-response.
